I've seen a lot of isekai bullshit lately. It seems like overnight a whole genre with a boatload of oddly videogame-centric tropes popped up from nowhere, and as with any fad you quickly find a lot of sameyness that gets old fast. Basically:

>protagonist is drawn into a fantastical parallel world

>fantasy frees protag from the unbearable decay of modern society

...Well, I'm not going to try to describe the genre via greentext, but that's the main thrust. The genre at its worst is shallow wish-fulfillment in the form of college dudes getting rich and famous playing videogames, but the upside is that there's usually a physicality that goes along with it, as the protagonist is suddenly having "near life experiences" and fighting for his life. When it's good (eg, Solo Leveling) it's an inspirational story of a dude working hard to improve himself, and finding that by working smart AND hard, he can make material gains.

When it's bad, it's just a bizarre abstraction of electronic gaming, which are themselves largely based on tabletop gaming, which in turn is a simulation of real life combat. It's more than a little perverse that there's been this fad (assuming it's a fad) of making abstractions of abstractions of life experience, rather than of the experience itself. Are our lives so empty that we now fantasize about getting to use "cheats" on MMOs?

That brings us to Solo Leveling. When it was recommended to me, I assumed from the name that it was yet more creatively bankrupt bottom-barrel trash, but I've found it to focus less on gamey bullshit, and more on its moderately interesting character arc, which involves black and grey morality as opposed to a near-messianic figure who is too modest to admit that he's the Goku of the story, and prefers to simply blunder into saving the world. Put another way, the protag is a kind of Nietzschean ubermensch, and we see him transvaluate some values.

It also has an implicit message that I like: stop being an NPC and do your daily 100 pushups, 100 situps, 100 squats, and 10k run.

As of chapter 35, I give it 8/10.
